coffee.subtitle: {from} – {to} · {min}-minute chats · online or in person · Eastern Time
coffee.step.1: Sign up: tell us who you are, your interests and what you'd like to talk about, plus where to meet — a café address or your meeting link.
coffee.step.2: Pick your times: in the two-week window, click (or drag, on a computer) the 15-minute slots when you're free.
coffee.step.3: Book: filter people by identity and goal, open someone's page, pick one of their free slots and add a line about why.
coffee.step.4: Wait for a yes: once accepted, you both see each other's email and contact. No yes means no meeting.
coffee.rule.1: A chat only happens once the other person accepts. If there's no yes by the start time, treat it as a no — please don't make a wasted trip.
coffee.rule.2: The host's location applies: their address for in-person chats, or their meeting link (shown after acceptance).
coffee.rule.3: Each chat is {min} minutes, all times Eastern (ET), with a buffer between slots.
coffee.rule.4: Once booked, a slot is gone for good (even if declined); booking closes {h} hours before the start.
coffee.rule.5: Once accepted, you both see each other's email and contact in case someone runs late. You can have up to {n} bookings awaiting an answer.

about.title: About YaleLink
about.intro: A community platform of our own. Open source, modular, dependency-free — we lay the foundation, everyone adds the features.
about.why1: WeChat groups are our default community, but they're closed, forgetful and hard to organize in. Alumni advice gets retold every year; job leads scatter across dozens of groups.
about.why2: With a Yale inbox as the first layer of trust we can build a better internal community: careers first, alumni resources linked precisely, events organized by region wherever you are.
about.why3: And keep ACSSY running steadily: playbooks, contacts and templates live on the platform; every event is a project with a lead, claimed tasks and visible progress, so the next team ramps up fast.
about.modulesSub: Generated from the module registry. Simple modules are one file; modules that write data are split into rules / API / UI.
about.apiSub: Listed automatically from code. The prototype implements these in the browser; a real backend implements the same list and the front-end modules stay unchanged.

about.how2: Add a module: write a one-page RFC, create js/modules/xxx.js calling registerModule(), add dictionary keys and data — the nav updates itself.
about.how3: Add content: jobs, events, guides, playbooks and templates are JSON under web/data/ — open a PR.
about.how4: Host events: ACSSY members start from a playbook and write the retro back into it.
